chapter_theme: The opening fifth of Pattinathar's Puranamalai, a garland of two-line confessions each closing on the address பூரணமே, the Fullness. The first ten stanzas climb the body from the root triangle to the crown, naming the deity or thing the poet failed to look at in each place (the Maiden, Brahma, Mal, Rudra, Mahesvara, Sadasiva, nada-bindu, the crown-space, the nose-tip, the two channels), and the rest name the worldly trusts that took the looking's place: family, wealth, the body held as lasting, women, land and gold, pilgrimage to Kasi instead of the breath, and the uncounted parents of past births.
structure_note: Every stanza has the same shape: a thing not seen (பாராமல், காணாமல், போற்றாமல்) in the first line and the loss it caused (அறிவழிந்தேன், பொறியழிந்தேன், கலங்கினேன்) in the second, ending பூரணமே. The reading of each is what it names as unseen. 674 to 683 follow the yogic body upward; 684 and 696 bracket the second half with the same first line, that the Lord walked within the flesh unseen.

674.reading: Not having praised the Maiden within the three-cornered chakra that rose at the root, the poet says he forgot his understanding.
674.nuance: மூலம் is the root centre and முக்கோண சக்கரம் its triangle, where tradition places the goddess as the coiled power; வாலை, the young goddess, is read by tradition as that power or the breath at the root, and the verse does not say which. The first stanza sets the addressee: பூரணம், the Fullness, is what all these failures were failures to see.

675.reading: Not having met and seen Brahma who stands risen in the lotus of the lower belly, the poet says he was ruined.
675.nuance: உந்தி usually means the navel, but since 676 gives the navel (நாவி) to Mal, tradition reads உந்தி here as the second centre (svadhishthana), whose presiding god is Brahma. The gods of the chakras are the creator, the preserver and the destroyer in ascending order, the Puranic trinity made into stages of the body.

676.reading: Not seeing tall Mal in the middle of the navel lotus, the poet says his life-breath was spoiled and his understanding lost.
676.nuance: நாவிக்கமலம் is the navel lotus (manipuraka), to which tradition assigns Vishnu. ஆவி கெட்டு, the breath or spirit spoiled, is the first of the chapter's losses to name the breath, which 694 will make the practice itself.

677.reading: Not seeing Rudra in the heart in truth, the poet says his purpose was lost and he was confused.
677.nuance: இருதயம், the heart centre (anahata), has Rudra as its god. உண்மையுடன் பாராமல் asks for a true seeing, not a doctrinal one; கருத்து, the lost thing, is the mind's purpose or intent.

678.reading: Not opening his eyes to see Mahesvara at the throat centre, the poet says he melted in hunger and his heart trembled.
678.nuance: விசுத்தி is the throat centre, named here by its Sanskrit name while the others are given by body-part; its god Mahesvara is the fourth in the ascending series. பசித்துருகி, melted in hunger, is a bodily hunger on the surface and, by the chapter's logic, hunger for what was not seen.

679.reading: Not seeing with understanding the stainless Sadasiva who has the eye in the brow, the poet says his senses were lost.
679.nuance: நெற்றி விழி, the eye in the brow, names the brow centre (ajna) and Siva's third eye at once; Sadasiva is its god, the fifth and highest of the series the chapter climbs. பொறி here, as in 680 and 689, is the senses or the faculties, lost by not seeing.

680.reading: Not seeing nada and bindu with care, the poet says his awareness was deluded and his senses lost.
680.nuance: After the five gods of the five centres the verse names no god but நாதம் and விந்து, sound and point, which the Tirumanthiram makes the first stage of manifestation above Sadasiva; tradition places them above the brow, below the crown. போதம், awareness, is the thing deluded.

681.reading: Not looking with firmness at the space at the crown, the poet says he lost his understanding in fear.
681.nuance: உச்சி வெளி, the space at the crown, is the top of the series begun at the root in 674; tradition calls it the thousand-petalled lotus or the void, and the verse calls it only space. அச்சமுடன், with fear, is the one emotion named in the ascent, set against உறுதியுடன், the firmness the looking needed.

682.reading: Not keeping his eyes open on the tip of the nose, the poet says his body was spoiled and his understanding lost.
682.nuance: முழித்திருந்து, staying with eyes open, makes the nose-tip gaze a waking watch and not a trance; the verse takes it as a thing to do, which Kakapusundar (2339) attacks as a false seat of the sushumna. ஆக்கை கெட்டு, the body spoiled, is the loss named for a bodily practice.

683.reading: Not able to know the nature of the ida and pingala channels, the poet says he hesitated with obstruction.
683.nuance: இடை and பிங்கலை are the left and right channels, sun and moon in the Siddhar cipher; இயல்பு, their nature, is their alternation, which the Tirumanthiram's வாரசரம் chapter teaches. தடை, obstruction, and தயங்கினேன், hesitated, describe a breath that would not move: the loss is in the practice itself.

684.reading: Not seeing you who stood and walked within the flesh, the poet says he lived as 'I' and lost his good.
684.nuance: நான் என்று இருந்து, staying as 'I', is the one cause the verse gives for not seeing the one who walked inside; the stanza turns the chapter from body-places to the self that failed to look. 696 repeats the first line with உடலுக்குள் for ஊனுக்குள்.

685.reading: Not trusting and desiring the true life and living it fully, the poet says he trusted the false life and lamented.
685.nuance: மெய்வாழ்வு and பொய்வாழ்வு, true life and false life, are left undefined; the stanzas that follow (686 to 689) list what the false life trusted in, so the pair reads as the inner life against the household one. புலம்பினேன், lamented, names the genre: the Puranamalai is itself a lament.

686.reading: Trusting that wife, children, father, mother and the kin that come with birth are real, the poet says his body was wasted.
686.nuance: உண்டு என்று நம்பி, trusting they exist, is the error named, not loving them: the kin are called unreal (not lasting) rather than bad. பிறவியுடன், with birth, marks them as what each birth brings and takes; 698 counts how many such parents there have been.

687.reading: Trusting that palanquins, litters and all possessions are real, the poet says his perception was lost.
687.nuance: தண்டிகை and பல்லாக்கு are the carried litter and palanquin, marks of rank; the poet whom tradition makes a rich merchant lists the furniture of his own former life. உணர்வு, perception, is what their trust cost.

688.reading: Bound in the belief that this body and life would always be permanent, the poet says he lost his footing.
688.nuance: சதம், permanent, is the word of the delusion, and பந்தம், bond, is the effect: belief in the body's lasting is itself the binding. பதம், the thing lost, is the state or standing one had.

689.reading: Fallen into the infatuation of women and the world, the poet says his awareness was deluded and his senses lost.
689.nuance: மாதர் பிரபஞ்சம் may be a pair, women and the world, or one phrase, the world of women; the second line is the same as 680's, so the delusion of desire and the failure to see nada and bindu have the same cost.

690.reading: Not looking to chariyai, kiriyai, yoga and jnana, the poet says his use was lost like a moon that has seen the sun.
690.nuance: The four Saiva paths are named as one thing neglected, not ranked; the chapter elsewhere prizes only the inner seeing, so the stanza is more orthodox than its neighbours. பரிதி கண்ட மதி, the moon that has seen the sun, is the moon paled at daybreak: the image is of a light that loses its use, not of a thing destroyed.

691.reading: Fallen into the infatuation of desire for land, women and gold, the poet says he was confused like a cow that has lost its eyes.
691.nuance: மண் பெண் பொன், land, woman, gold, is the fixed triad of desires in Tamil devotional verse, which Pattinathar uses elsewhere; the blind cow (கண்கெட்ட மாடு) wanders without direction, the picture of a desire that cannot see where it goes.

692.reading: Not seeing the sole First One and living alone with it, the poet says he was born here unjustly and stood wandering.
692.nuance: தனி முதல், the sole first, and தனித்திருந்து, staying alone, answer each other: the one is seen by one who is alone. அநியாயமாய்ப் பிறந்து, born unjustly or to no purpose, calls the birth itself the waste.

693.reading: Not examining and seeing the one who stood within the twelve cool kalas and danced, the poet says his understanding was lost.
693.nuance: ஈராறு தண்கலை, the twelve cool kalas, is cipher: the kalas are the digits of the moon and of the breath, and twelve is the sun's count in the Tirumanthiram (856), while தண், cool, is the moon's epithet; tradition takes it as the breath's measure, the twelve finger-breadths of the outgoing breath, in which the Lord dances. The dance (கூத்து) within the body is Tirumular's.

694.reading: Not watching the breath and praising you in gladness, the poet says he went as far as Kasi and wandered until his legs were weary.
694.nuance: வாசி, the breath as practice, is set against காசி, the pilgrimage city, in a rhyme that carries the argument: the one is within and free, the other far and tiring. காலலுத்தேன், my legs grew tired, is the physical cost, repeated at 696 for the hill shrines; the verse is the chapter's clearest statement that the practice replaces the pilgrimage.

695.reading: Not seeing with both eyes the one who mingled with the ninety-six instruments and played, the poet says he lost his standing.
695.nuance: கருவிகள் தொண்ணூற்றாறு, the ninety-six instruments, is the Tamil Saiva count of the tattvas and their adjuncts that make up the embodied person; the verse does not list them. இருவிழியால், with the two eyes, may be plain (the bodily eyes) or coded (the sun and moon, the two channels); ஈடு, the thing lost, is one's worth or standing.

696.reading: Not seeing you who stood and walked within the body, the poet says he wandered over every forest and hill until his legs were weary.
696.nuance: The first line repeats 684 with the body (உடல்) for the flesh (ஊன்); கடமலை தோறும், over every forest and hill, is the pilgrim's road to hill shrines, so the stanza pairs with 694's Kasi: the one walked inside while the poet walked outside.

697.reading: Saying that in every land and time we shall remain without dying, and not looking closely at you, the poet says he lost his form.
697.nuance: இறவாதிருப்பம், we shall not die, is the unspoken belief of ordinary life put into words; உருவழிந்தேன், lost my form, is the plain answer, the body gone. The stanza may also be read as a jibe at those who seek deathlessness in the wrong place, since 968 and 1033 claim it from the breath.

698.reading: The poet asks how many fathers and mothers he has been with, born and dying among them as a madman.
698.nuance: எத்தனை தாய் தந்தை, how many mothers and fathers, turns 686's kin into a count across births: each birth had its own parents, and the stanza asks for the total. பித்தன், madman, is the poet's name for the one who kept being born; 702 gives the number of births as eighty-four lakh.

links.note: Tirumular says that taking up ida and pingala and twisting at the root in the triangle (மூலத்து முக்கோணத்துள்) one may see the Lord's feet; Pattinathar names the three-cornered chakra risen at the root as the place where the Maiden was not praised. The same triangle at the root is the practice's starting point in both; Tirumular gives the method, Pattinathar the omission.

Tirumular puts the supreme Shakti and the truth above the adharas, beyond the sixteen; Pattinathar's climb ends past the six centres and nada-bindu at the crown-space (உச்சி வெளி). Both place the goal above the named centres rather than in any of them.

Kakapusundar says that those who stare at the nose-tip calling it the sushumna wander in vain like madmen and perish, and moves the seat to the uvula; Pattinathar counts not keeping his eyes open on the nose-tip among the failures that spoiled his body. On the reading that 682 recommends the nose-tip gaze as a practice, the two disagree about whether it is the way or a false way.

Tirumular says that with both gazes set at the middle of the nose there is no withering, no ruin for the house and no self, and we become Siva; Pattinathar says that for not watching the nose-tip his body was spoiled and his understanding lost. The gain in the one is the loss in the other, the same practice seen from its two sides.

Tirumular says moon and sun rise and fall through ida and pingala over the two fortnights and life wells up in the middle, and tells the reader to understand and discern it; Pattinathar says that not knowing the nature (இயல்பு) of ida and pingala he hesitated with obstruction. The nature Tirumular teaches is what Pattinathar says he lacked.

The Kural says the friendship of body and life is like a bird flying off and leaving its shell; Pattinathar says he was bound by believing this body and life would be permanent. Both deny the bond between body and life any permanence; the Kural states it as a fact, Pattinathar as the error he lived by.

Tirumular matches the four paths to four kinds of people, devotees in chariyai, servants in kiriyai, yogis and siddhas in jnana; Pattinathar names the same four, chariyai, kiriyai, yoga and jnana, as what he failed to look to. Both hold the four as the whole of the way; Pattinathar does not rank them, Tirumular does.

Sivavakkiyar calls those who run through town, country and forest searching 'mutes' and tells them to know the Supreme straight within themselves; Pattinathar says he wandered as far as Kasi, legs weary, instead of watching the breath. Both set the search outside against the one within; Pattinathar names the inner thing as the breath (வாசி), Sivavakkiyar as the Supreme spread everywhere.

Pattinathar names the breath (வாசி) as the thing to watch instead of going to Kasi, without saying what it is; Kakapusundar defines it: what comes and goes is the vaasi, and so are the sun and moon in the sky, and the siddha is the one of clear mind. The definition fills in what Pattinathar's rhyme only names.

Tirumular counts the countless tattvas down to the ninety-six and then to the twenty-five; Pattinathar names the ninety-six instruments as the field in which the Lord mingles and plays, unseen. The count is Tirumular's; Pattinathar does not reduce it but puts the Lord inside it.

Tirumular says the six sects standing in the assembly do not see the God who stands within the body; Pattinathar says that not seeing the one who walked within the body he wandered over every forest and hill. Both put the unseen God in the body and the seekers outside it; Tirumular blames the sects, Pattinathar himself.
698 asks how many mothers and fathers the poet has been born to and died among; 702 answers with the traditional count, eighty-four lakh births, and the wound they left.

source_issues: The verses are printed without word division (each line is one unbroken string), so some readings depend on where the words are cut; 684 ஊனுக்குணீநின்று is ஊனுக்குள் நீ நின்று with the ள் lost in the sandhi, and 696 gives the undamaged form உடலுக்குள்நீநின்று.
676 ends அறிவழிந்தென்பூரணமே where every other stanza has அறிவழிந்தேன்; the ன் for ேன் is a copying slip.
